title: Projective Extensions and the Little Group Method

items.title: Normalized projective representations and their factor sets
items.statement: For a finite group Q and a nonzero finite-dimensional complex space V, a normalized projective representation is P:Q→GL(V), P(1)=1, with P(q)P(r)=α(q,r)P(qr), α(q,r)∈C×. Fixed-factor equivalence means simultaneous linear conjugacy, not arbitrary scalar rephasing. Irreducible means having no proper nonzero common invariant subspace. Define normalized scalar two-cocycles by α(q,r)α(qr,t)=α(q,rt)α(r,t), α(1,q)=α(q,1)=1, with trivial Q-action on C×.

references.title: Späth Definition 1.4 and cocycle paragraph, pp.2–3

items.title: Associativity gives the normalized cocycle identity
items.statement: The uniquely determined factor set of a normalized projective representation is a normalized scalar two-cocycle.

references.title: Späth immediately after Definition 1.4, p.3

items.proof_strategy: Expand (P(q)P(r))P(t)=P(q)(P(r)P(t)); cancel the invertible P(qrt). P(1)=1 gives both normalization identities. Nonzero space is needed for scalar uniqueness.

items.title: Rephasing and scalar coboundaries
items.statement: For c:Q→C× with c(1)=1, P′(q)=c(q)P(q) has factor α′=α δc, where δc(q,r)=c(q)c(r)/c(qr). Normalized cocycles form an abelian group under pointwise multiplication, and the δc form a subgroup. Rephasing preserves invariant subspaces and fixed-factor intertwining maps when applied simultaneously.

references.title: Späth cocycle paragraph and Remark 1.5(a), p.3

items.proof_strategy: Multiply the two rephased operators. Verify the cocycle identity for δc by cancellation; δ(cd)=δc δd, δ1=1, and δ(c⁻¹)=(δc)⁻¹. Pointwise products and inverses preserve the cocycle equations. Distinguish rephasing from similarity.

items.title: The twisted group algebra
items.statement: For a normalized scalar two-cocycle α on finite Q, C^α[Q] is the complex vector space with basis u_q and bilinear product u_q u_r=α(q,r)u_qr. Its unit is u_1; associativity and invertibility of the basis elements are verified in the next lemma.

references.title: Späth Remark 1.5(b), p.3

items.title: Twisted algebra modules and projective representations
items.statement: The displayed twisted product is associative and unital. Each u_q is invertible with inverse α(q,q⁻¹)⁻¹u_q⁻¹. Nonzero finite-dimensional unital C^α[Q]-modules correspond exactly to normalized α-projective representations, preserving submodules, intertwiners, and irreducibility. The regular module gives an α-projective representation of dimension |Q|.

references.title: Späth Remark 1.5(b), p.3

items.proof_strategy: Check associativity on three basis elements and use the cocycle identity to equate α(q,q⁻¹) and α(q⁻¹,q). Extend operators linearly in one direction and act by u_q in the other. The two constructions are inverse on objects and maps; regular left multiplication proves existence.

items.title: Associated projective extension of a normal type
items.statement: Fix finite G, N normal in G, ρ:N→GL(S) irreducible over C, and I=I_G(χρ). An associated projective inertia extension P:I→GL(S) satisfies P|N=ρ, P(ng)=ρ(n)P(g), and P(gn)=P(g)ρ(n). Linear extension retains the published definition specialized to I. These are maps on I; no assertion that P itself descends to I/N is made.

references.title: Späth Definitions 1.6–1.7, p.3

items.title: Construction of the projective inertia extension
items.statement: Every irreducible complex N-type admits an associated projective inertia extension. Its factor set is the inflation of a normalized two-cocycle α on Q=I/N. It satisfies P(g)ρ(n)P(g)⁻¹=ρ(gng⁻¹).

references.title: Späth Definition 1.7 existence paragraph and Lemma 1.8(a–c), pp.3–4

items.proof_strategy: Choose a section s:Q→I with s(1)=1. Choose T_q with T_qρ(n)T_q⁻¹=ρ(s(q)ns(q)⁻¹), T_1=1. Put d(q,r)=s(q)s(r)s(qr)⁻¹∈N. Schur gives T_qT_r=α(q,r)ρ(d(q,r))T_qr. Define P(ns(q))=ρ(n)T_q. Expand products to prove P(g)P(h)=α(gN,hN)P(gh), both N-covariance identities, and normalization. The cocycle lemma now applies. T_q alone is generally not a projective representation of Q: the ρ(d(q,r)) term cannot be discarded.

items.title: Choice independence of associated extensions
items.statement: If P and P′ extend the same concrete ρ, then P′(g)=c(gN)P(g) for a unique normalized c:Q→C×. If their restrictions are merely equivalent, first conjugate by a fixed N-isomorphism. The quotient factor sets differ by δc. This includes a change of section and all intertwiner choices. If Z is normal in I and contained in kerρ, then P descends to I/Z and is associated to the type on N/Z.

references.title: Späth Lemma 1.8(d) and its full proof, pp.3–4

items.proof_strategy: Both P(g) and P′(g) implement conjugation by g. Their ratio commutes with ρ(N), hence is scalar. N-covariance makes that scalar constant on cosets; equality on N normalizes it. Apply the rephasing formula. For the last claim, P(gz)=P(g)ρ(z)=P(g); the covariance equations descend.

items.title: The Clifford obstruction class
items.statement: Define H²(Q,C×)=Z²(Q,C×)/B²(Q,C×) using the normalized scalar groups already proved above, with trivial coefficient action. The Clifford obstruction of ρ is [α], where α is the quotient factor set of an associated projective inertia extension. The preceding choice lemma makes this independent of section, intertwiners, and the isomorphic model of ρ. This is the explicit factor-set quotient, with no appeal to derived cohomology, Schur multipliers, or universal covers.

references.title: Späth cocycle paragraph p.3 and Lemma 1.8(d), pp.3–4

items.title: Vanishing of the obstruction characterizes extension
items.statement: ρ extends linearly to I if and only if [α]=1 in H²(I/N,C×). The vanishing condition is equivalent to α δc=1 for a normalized c. This holds also for I=N and I=G.

references.title: Späth Definition 1.7 and Lemma 1.8(d), pp.3–4; vanishing criterion derived explicitly

items.proof_strategy: If α δc=1, rephase P by c∘π; it is multiplicative and unchanged on N. Conversely a genuine extension is an associated projective extension with factor 1, so the choice lemma expresses 1=α δc. Neither direction assumes that invariance alone implies extension.

items.title: Finite-valued representatives for scalar cocycles
items.statement: If |Q|=m and α is a normalized C×-valued cocycle, α is cohomologous to a cocycle β taking values in μ_m. More precisely, [α]^m=1, and if its order is e then an equivalent μ_e-valued cocycle exists. H²(Q,C×) is finite.

references.title: Mendonça Theorem 1.2.2(a–c), pp.5–6, specialized to K=C

items.proof_strategy: Put d(q)=∏_{t∈Q}α(q,t). Multiply the cocycle equation over t to obtain α(q,r)^m=d(q)d(r)/d(qr). Choose c(q)^m=d(q)⁻¹ with c(1)=1 and set β=α δc. For exact order e use α^e=δd_e in the identical root argument. There are only finitely many μ_m-valued functions on Q×Q, so their classes form a finite set. Only finitely many root choices are needed.

items.title: The cocycle central extension
items.statement: For a normalized cocycle α:Q×Q→D≤C×, Eα=Q×D with (q,a)(r,b)=(qr,α(q,r)ab) is a group with identity (1,1), inverse (q,a)⁻¹=(q⁻¹,α(q,q⁻¹)⁻¹a⁻¹), and central kernel {1}×D over Q. D may be infinite; Eα is finite when D is finite.

references.title: Späth Proposition 1.11 and Theorem 1.12 proof, pp.4–5

items.proof_strategy: Expand triple products, apply cocycle identity, check both inverse products using α(q,q⁻¹)=α(q⁻¹,q), then verify exactness and centrality. Do not apply finite-group Maschke to Q×C×.

items.title: Linearization with a prescribed central character
items.statement: For a character χ:D→C×, projective representations R of Q with factor χ∘α correspond to linear representations L of Eα with L(1,a)=χ(a)Id by L(q,a)=χ(a)R(q). Inverses take R(q)=L(q,1). This preserves subspaces and maps. In particular α-linearization uses χ(a)=a, and α⁻¹-linearization uses χ(a)=a⁻¹. Rephasing first gives a finite central group.

references.title: Späth Theorem 1.12(b), Corollary 1.13, pp.4–5; inverse central character made explicit

items.proof_strategy: Check the product on both sides against the multiplication of Eα. Recovery and intertwiner equivalence follow by factoring (q,a)=(1,a)(q,1). Apply finite-valued rephasing only when a finite group is needed.

items.title: Complete reducibility for finite twisted group algebras
items.statement: Every finite-dimensional complex module over C^α[Q], for finite Q and normalized scalar cocycle α, is completely reducible. In particular its regular module is semisimple.
items.proof_strategy: Rephase α to a root-of-unity-valued β, preserving all invariant subspaces. Linearize over the finite central extension Q×μ_|Q| and apply the published finite-group complete reducibility theorem. Each invariant complement remains invariant for the projective operators, and undoing scalar rephasing preserves it. Transport through the twisted-module dictionary. No Maschke argument is applied to an infinite C×-central extension.

references.title: Späth Theorem 1.12 pp.4–5, finite central linearization, together with local finite-group complete reducibility

items.title: The inverse-factor action on the multiplicity space
items.statement: For an associated P on S with quotient factor α and a θ-isotypical finite-dimensional I-module U with action D, M=Hom_N(S,U) carries the α⁻¹-projective action R(gN)f=D(g)fP(g)⁻¹. It is independent of the lift g. Evaluation S⊗M→U intertwines P⊗R with D, and I-submodules and I-maps correspond to R-stable subspaces and intertwining maps.

references.title: Späth Theorem 1.15(a–c), pp.5–6; full local proof via published evaluation lemma

items.proof_strategy: Use the conjugation identity to check N-linearity. Replacing g by ng leaves the Hom action unchanged by N-linearity. Compute R(gN)R(hN)f=α(gN,hN)⁻¹D(gh)fP(gh)⁻¹. Evaluation is the published isotypical isomorphism. The published subspace and map assertions imply the claimed correspondence, since P(g) is invertible.

items.title: Projective Clifford correspondence
items.statement: Fix ρ, I, Q and associated P with factor α. Isomorphism classes of irreducible α⁻¹-projective Q-representations R biject with Irr(I|θ), via P⊗R inflated to I; induction then bijects with Irr(G|θ). Parameters are up to simultaneous similarity at fixed α, not arbitrary projective equivalence. The dimension upstairs is [G:I] dim(S) dim(R). Trivial Q gives S, trivial factor gives Gallagher, and I=G makes induction identity.

references.title: Späth Theorem 1.15 pp.5–6 and Corollary 1.13 p.5; local proof replaces cited Navarro proof

items.proof_strategy: Cancel α against α⁻¹ to get a linear tensor action. For each irreducible inertia module restriction is θ-isotypical; the multiplicity lemma supplies R and evaluation, proves irreducibility in both directions and injectivity on classes. Apply ordinary Clifford correspondence. Central proof device: after finite rephasing, on the pullback Ĩ=I×μ_m the maps (g,a)↦aP(g) and (g,a)↦a⁻¹R(gN) are linear; their tensor has trivial μ_m action and descends to I. This verifies precisely the central-character cancellation, without assuming a Schur cover. Dimension follows from the coset model of induction in the cited Clifford proof.

items.title: Canonical extension in the split abelian case
items.statement: For finite G=A⋊H with A abelian and λ∈Irr(A), λ is one-dimensional. If Hλ is its stabilizer under {}^hλ(a)=λ(h⁻¹ah), then I_G(λ)=A⋊Hλ and λ̃(a,h)=λ(a) is a linear extension. Its associated factor set is identically one.

references.title: tom Dieck Proposition 1.6.1 pp.20–21 and Proposition 4.2.6 p.57

items.proof_strategy: Each A-operator commutes with A, hence is scalar by Schur, and irreducibility makes the space one-dimensional. Compute conjugation and the stabilizer. Invariance under h and h⁻¹ are equivalent; λ(a h(b))=λ(a)λ(b) proves multiplicativity of λ̃ in the semidirect law.

items.title: The little-group method for finite split abelian kernels
items.statement: Choose one λ from each H-orbit in Irr(A) for finite G=A⋊H. For each λ and each irreducible ordinary complex representation τ of Hλ, Ind_{A⋊Hλ}^G(λ̃⊗Inf τ) is irreducible; these give each irreducible G-module exactly once. Its degree is [H:Hλ] dim τ. The projective correction is trivial for this canonical extension; in nonsplit general inertia the preceding theorem requires the inverse factor. Include A=1, H=1, trivial λ, and full stabilizer.

references.title: tom Dieck Remark 4.2.7 p.57

items.proof_strategy: Use the canonical extension to specialize projective Clifford correspondence to α=1, identifying I/A with Hλ. Clifford orbit partition proves uniqueness and exhaustivity. Coset counts give the degree. Verify the listed degeneracies directly from the formulas.

title: Projective Extensions and the Little Group Method — Examples

items.title: Quaternion matrices and the nontrivial quotient factor set
items.statement: For Q=(F₂)² and lifts s(a,b)=i^a j^b in Q8, the section cocycle is α((a,b),(c,d))=(-1)^(ac+bd+bc). With X=diag(i,-i), Y=[[0,1],[-1,0]], P(a,b)=X^aY^b is α-projective and linearizes to the faithful irreducible two-dimensional representation of Eα≅Q8 over D={±1}.

references.title: tom Dieck §4.3 problem 1 p.59, quaternion matrices; explicit quotient cocycle derived here

items.proof_strategy: Use X²=Y²=-Id and YX=-XY to verify the factor formula, including all carry terms. Map ((a,b),ε) to εi^a j^b to identify groups and εX^aY^b to identify representations. X has two distinct eigenspaces and Y exchanges them, proving irreducibility. Eight distinct matrices prove faithfulness.

items.title: An invariant character that does not extend
items.statement: The character λ of N={±1}≤Q8 with λ(-1)=-1 is invariant but has no linear extension to Q8. Its Clifford obstruction in H²((C₂)²,C×) is nontrivial.

references.title: Späth invariant-but-not-extendible discussion p.2; explicit quaternion witness calculated locally

items.proof_strategy: An extension has dimension one. Since [i,j]=-1, any homomorphism Q8→C× sends -1 to 1, contradiction. Independently the factor α has α((1,0),(0,1))=1 and α((0,1),(1,0))=-1; every scalar coboundary on an abelian Q is symmetric, so it cannot be killed. Use the vanishing criterion.

items.title: All irreducibles of the dihedral group of order 2n
items.statement: For n≥3, D_{2n}=C_n⋊C₂ with inversion, λ_k(r)=ζ_n^k is paired with λ_{-k}. If n is odd there are two linear irreducibles and (n-1)/2 degree-two irreducibles. If n is even there are four linear irreducibles and n/2-1 degree-two irreducibles. For two-element orbits, r↦diag(ζ_n^k,ζ_n^-k), s↦[[0,1],[1,0]]. Fixed characters k=0 and, for even n, k=n/2 extend with s↦±1.

references.title: tom Dieck Remark 4.2.7 p.57 and cyclic character paragraph p.20, explicit dihedral application

items.proof_strategy: List stabilizers: C₂ for k=-k mod n and 1 otherwise. Apply the little-group theorem and compute induction on the two cosets. Verify r^n=s²=1 and srs=r⁻¹ in the matrices. Degree squares sum to 2n in both cases. Interpret n=1,2 separately as C₂ and C₂×C₂ if that semidirect-product convention is used; do not call them faithful polygon symmetries.

items.title: Changing quaternion lifts and rephasing
items.statement: For the quaternion factor α on (F₂)² choose c(a,b)=(-1)^(ab). Then δc((a,b),(c,d))=(-1)^(ad+bc), and P′(a,b)=c(a,b)P(a,b) has factor α′=(-1)^(ac+bd+ad). Both describe the same obstruction; their ordered cross terms are interchanged.

references.title: Späth Remark 1.5(a), p.3, explicit quaternion calculation

items.proof_strategy: Expand ab+cd+(a+c)(b+d) in F₂. Multiply α by δc and check P′(1,1)=-XY corresponds to changing the lift k to -k. The asymmetric commutator ratio persists, so rephasing does not remove the nontrivial class.
